story.title: Two American Economists Awarded Nobel Prize for Economic Models
story.summary: Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford have been awarded the Nobel Prize in economics for their contributions to developing models that assist governments and central banks in managing economic shocks and stabilizing fluctuations in the economy. Their work focuses on smoothing boom-and-bust cycles to mitigate issues like unemployment and inflation.

timeline_highlights.title: Francis Halzen Awarded Nobel Prize in Physics for Neutrino Research
timeline_highlights.summary: Belgian physicist Francis Halzen has been awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics for his groundbreaking work on the IceCube Neutrino Observatory, which detects high-energy neutrinos from space, often referred to as 'ghost particles.' His research has significantly advanced the field of neutrino astronomy since its inception in the 1980s.

Halzen's work involves the detection of high-energy neutrinos from space.

explore_lenses.label: Why does this award matter for policy?
explore_lenses.title: It recognizes the framework behind modern stabilization analysis
explore_lenses.summary: Hall and Woodford’s work links economy-wide outcomes to forward-looking decisions by households and firms. That structure is central to how policymakers analyze tradeoffs among inflation, output and employment after shocks.

claims.text: The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences awarded the 2026 economics prize to Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford for “microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation.”
The Academy says New Keynesian models resulting from this research are used by central banks and finance ministries to quantify how stabilization policy affects business cycles.
Federal Reserve materials describe its FRB/US model as a large-scale New Keynesian model in which policy works importantly through households’, firms’ and investors’ expectations.
The practical implication is not that a model mechanically dictates an interest-rate decision: Fed staff use model scenarios alongside forecasts, other analysis and policymakers’ judgment.

explore_lenses.label: How did their ideas reshape economics?
explore_lenses.title: They replaced fixed relationships with decision-based models
explore_lenses.summary: The prize traces a shift away from relying mainly on stable historical correlations between macroeconomic variables. Hall emphasized forward-looking consumption decisions, while Woodford’s work helped put interest rates, pricing behavior and expectations at the center of monetary-policy analysis.

claims.text: The Academy says traditional Keynesian models assumed relatively stable statistical links among variables such as inflation, unemployment, consumption and output; the 1970s oil crises exposed how unreliable those relationships could be.
Hall’s 1978 research modeled consumption as depending on households’ expectations of their long-run resources, rather than only on current income.
NPR’s account of the prize says Woodford focused on firms’ pricing decisions and the role of expectations, while the Academy credits the pair with laying the basis for the New Keynesian approach.

The Academy’s view is that these microfounded models marked a paradigm shift because aggregate outcomes are built from many household and business choices rather than imposed as fixed economy-wide correlations.

explore_lenses.label: What does this mean for future crises?
explore_lenses.title: Expectations and communication remain central—and contested
explore_lenses.summary: The work reinforces why central banks explain their goals and expected policy paths: public expectations can affect spending, hiring, pricing and borrowing before policy fully takes effect. But economists still debate how precisely authorities can steer those expectations in real-world conditions.

claims.text: The Federal Reserve says clear, systematic policy communication helps households and firms plan and can reduce destabilizing policy surprises.
The Fed’s policy principles say policymakers may need to act forward-lookingly because changes in financial conditions can affect inflation and employment later rather than immediately.
Forecast: The Royal Swedish Academy says the models will continue to be refined as economies change, rather than serving as a final or fixed policy template.

Researchers Stefano Eusepi and Bruce Preston of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York argue that standard New Keynesian prescriptions often assume precise management of expectations, while post-financial-crisis experience has raised questions about that assumption.

story_report.summary: The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences awarded the 2026 economics prize to Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford for “microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation.” Their research helped establish New Keynesian models used by central banks and finance ministries to assess how stabilization policies may affect business cycles. The immediate practical consequence is a stronger analytical framework for examining responses to shocks, inflation and employment risks, although policymakers use model results alongside forecasts, other analysis and judgment rather than as automatic instructions.

sections.heading: Foundations of New Keynesian Models
sections.body: The Academy says older Keynesian models often relied on stable statistical relationships among inflation, unemployment, consumption and output, assumptions tested by the oil crises of the 1970s. Hall’s 1978 work treated household consumption as a function of expected long-run resources rather than only current income. Woodford’s work focused on firms’ pricing decisions and expectations; together, the pair laid foundations for an approach that builds economy-wide outcomes from household and business choices.

sections.heading: Policy Communication and Model Limits
sections.body: Federal Reserve policy principles say clear, systematic communication can help households and businesses plan and reduce destabilizing surprises, while policy may need to be forward-looking because financial conditions affect inflation and employment with delays. Federal Reserve materials describe its FRB/US system as a large-scale New Keynesian model in which expectations matter. However, New York Fed researchers Stefano Eusepi and Bruce Preston argue that standard prescriptions can assume policymakers can manage expectations with greater precision than post-financial-crisis experience supports.

unresolved.text: Models can organize evidence and test policy scenarios, but they cannot resolve uncertainty over the size, source or duration of a new shock, or guarantee how households and firms will interpret policy actions. The Academy expects the models to continue being refined as economies change.

related_stories.title: New York City Police Use-of-Force Review Ordered by Mayor Mamdani
related_stories.summary: Mayor Zohran Mamdani has ordered a review of the New York Police Department's use-of-force policies, marking the first such review in a decade. This decision comes amid calls for greater police reform, although city officials state that it is not directly related to a recent police response to an ICE shooting. The review aims to address concerns raised by progressive advocates regarding police practices.
